passage: When Ms Iyer called Varun to read aloud from the English reader, he stood with the book close to his face and started blinking fast, again and again. From the next bench Nitin whispered, “He didn't even look at it last night, see how his eyes are going.” Ms Iyer heard. “Blinking doesn't tell us that, Nitin. Many people blink more when they're nervous or tired.” She turned back. “Take your time, Varun.” Varun took a breath, put a finger under the line and read on more slowly. By the third sentence the blinking had eased.

qa.q: What might Varun have been feeling while he blinked, and what else could explain it?
qa.a: Most likely nervous about reading in front of the class, since it eased once he slowed down and put a finger under the line. Tiredness can also make people blink more.

qa.q: What did Ms Iyer do that helped?
qa.a: She told the class that blinking does not show what Nitin claimed, and she gave Varun time, which let him settle. 🙂

qa.q: How might Nitin see it after Ms Iyer's words?
qa.a: He may realise he jumped to a conclusion from a cue with many causes, and perhaps feel a little embarrassed.

grounding: A child blinks a lot when nervous reading aloud, which a classmate reads as not having prepared.

passage:
“Read your poem for me, Vishal.”
“Okay.” Vishal held the notebook and blinked, blink, blink, blink.
“Why are you blinking so much?” said Usha. “Did you copy it?”
“No! I wrote it.”
“Your eyes are going like a butterfly.”
Vishal rubbed them. “I'm nervous. And they're tired from the screen lesson.”
Usha put the notebook down. “I'm sorry. I shouldn't decide from your eyes. Read slowly, I'm listening.”
He read. The poem was about a crow in the monsoon.

qa.a: It was about a crow in the monsoon.

qa.q: What was Vishal probably feeling when he said “No! I wrote it”?
qa.a: Hurt and nervous about being doubted, since he right away explained the blinking as nerves and tired eyes. He may also have felt worried his poem would not be liked.

qa.q: What did Usha do that repaired the moment?
qa.a: She apologised, stopped judging by his eyes and listened, which let him read without extra pressure.

qa.q: What would change if Usha had kept believing he copied?
qa.a: Vishal might feel distrusted and be even more nervous next time, and the poem would go unheard.

grounding: A child blinks from nerves and tiredness; blinking is not evidence of dishonesty.
